doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

title: Speaking to the audience about the music
summary: Palmer urges musicians to explain their tunes; Rowe recalls Cannonball Adderley.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. That’s another thing is, yeah I don’t want to go too deep into it but just being able to relate to the audience outside of just playing. You know when you play a tune, explain what the tune is. Explain the name of it, if it has a story it’s just going to inform them and maybe they’ll imagine it differently when they hear it. So you know I think it would benefit us greatly to have the ability to be able to speak about the music that we make, that we compose. You know we’ve got to able to give a 30-second elevator speech as to why we should have our band hired. You know? Or what makes it great? You know. So you know when I go hear a band and they just play the whole time and not say anything to the audience, I mean that’s happened before. And I get it, I mean some people are quiet. You know I even play, I play in certain bands with certain leaders who are very quiet and you know, even me, I’ll just say the leader’s name at the end of the concert. Ba- ba-ba. Check him out, yeah and everybody claps. But yeah just a few words about what you do I think goes a long way and it helps sell the music. You know? You say, “I wrote a song about my three cats and we’re going to play it right now and it’s on my new record.” And the at the end of the concert somebody comes up to you and says, “We really liked that cat song, and we’ve got some cats at home, can I buy your record?”
It reminds me of the three times I saw Cannonball Adderley years ago. He was a master of that.
